summary: A US think tank says China's AI computing power will nearly double next year but still leans on US chips, and young travellers are buying clothes to wear once.
body: China's available computing power for AI is expected to roughly double in 2027, from about 4.6 million to 8.8 million "H100-equivalents", a unit based on a leading Nvidia chip, according to a report by the Institute for Progress, a Washington think tank, reported by the South China Morning Post [^1][^2]. The report estimates about 65% of that capacity will still come from US-designed chips, counting legal imports, smuggled processors and computers rented remotely in other countries, mostly in Southeast Asia [^2]. It says the US has about 16 times more AI training compute, yet China's best models trail US ones by only about 6.5 months [^1][^2]. The authors argue for tighter US controls; that is a policy view, and Chinese firms are working to build their own alternatives [^1][^2]. My read: China's AI progress still depends on hardware it does not fully control, which is why chips sit at the centre of US-China tension.

In daily life, young Chinese travellers are buying cipaoyi, or "disposable outfits": cheap clothes, often under 50 yuan (about US$7), bought for one trip or photo shoot and then thrown away or resold, Sixth Tone reports [^3]. Posts about the trend on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, have drawn more than 60 million views, and it took off during the National Day holiday [^3]. A 20-year-old student says it lets her travel on a budget and resell the clothes afterwards [^3]. Dermatologists warn that low-quality dyes and stiff fabrics can irritate skin, and a recycling firm says textile collections nearly doubled over the holiday, some with tags still attached [^3]. A circular-economy association projects China will discard 50 million tonnes of clothing a year by 2030 [^3].
